summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's intrinsic behavior, style, or format — teaching it tasks or domain patterns that prompting alone cannot reliably enforce — whereas RAG is the right choice when you need the model to reference current, proprietary, or frequently changing knowledge. Prompt engineering should always be your first attempt because it is cheapest and fastest; only escalate to fine-tuning once prompts plateau and you have hundreds to thousands of high-quality examples. In practice, many production systems combine a lightly fine-tuned model (for consistent behavior) with RAG (for fresh facts).
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent output format, tone, or domain-specific behavior that few-shot prompting cannot reliably reproduce across many requests.
Choose fine-tuning when you have a stable task with hundreds to thousands of labeled examples and want to reduce prompt length, latency, and per-call cost.
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when the required knowledge changes frequently or must be auditable and traceable to source documents.
Prefer prompt engineering first when the task can be solved with instructions and a few examples, since it is the fastest and cheapest path to validate feasibility.
